question: How long did creation take?
summary: Genesis 1:3-2:3 presents creation unfolding across six distinct days with a seventh day of rest. Genesis 2:4 refers to the whole thing happening in a single 'day' (beyom in Hebrew) when God made the earth and the heavens.

reconcile.connective: Defenders deny any clash over duration: the Hebrew yom in Genesis 2:4 is the idiomatic "when," a summary covering the whole six-day week, not a rival one-day creation.

discrepancy.connective: Source critics, classically Julius Wellhausen, argue Genesis 2:4 belongs to a separate (J) account whose single-"day" framing was never meant to be squared with the six-day schema of the Priestly account in Genesis 1.

link.title: GotQuestions: Does Genesis chapter 1 mean literal 24-hour days?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment of the meaning of yom, including Genesis 2:4's use of 'day' for an unspecified time period.

excerpts.excerpt_text: The Hebrew yom can refer to daylight (1:5a), to a 24-hour period (1:5b), or to an unspecified time period (2:4b, “When,” literally in the day; cp. Exod 20:8-11).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly distinguishes the senses of the very word at issue, stating that the 'day' of 2:4b is an unspecified time period ('When'), not the same as a 24-hour creation day — the precise hinge of the contradiction.
excerpts.source_note_text: 1:5 God called (or named): To name something is to exercise authority over it (see also 2:19-20). • day: The Hebrew yom can refer to daylight (1:5a), to a 24-hour period (1:5b), or to an unspecified time period (2:4b, “When,” literally in the day; cp. Exod 20:8-11). • evening . . . morning: The Hebrew day began at sundown, just as the first day began with darkness and brought the first morning light.
